newsitem.title: UK: Feisty Spice Girls land two top Brit pop awards.
newsitem.headline: Feisty Spice Girls land two top Brit pop awards.

text.p: The Spice Girls, a feisty quintet who boast Margaret Thatcher as their role model, on Monday took two of the top honours at the annual Brit pop awards.
The ultimate girl gang, who have topped the charts in 31 countries, hit the big time this month when going to number one in the United States with their first single, a feat that eluded the Beatles.

But they had to share the Brit Award limelight at the glittering gala with the Manic Street Preachers, a Welsh rock group making a triumphant comeback after the disappearance of their 28-year-old lyricist Richey Edwards.
Edwards, an alcoholic and anorexic who was being treated for depression, vanished in 1995.
His empty car was found abandoned on a motorway near the famed Severn Bridge. He has never officially been declared dead.
But for the booming 2.5 billion pound ($4 billion) pop industry, the Spice Girls were the stars of the night with their raucous, scantily dressed dance routines.
They took the award for best single of the year for "Wannabe" which proved an instant international hit.
"Say You'll be There" also won top video with the raunchy quintet telling fans: "We are proof you can win with a little help from girl power."

Comedian compere Ben Elton jokingly apologised for the absence of former premier Thatcher, telling top record executives at their annual celebration: "Thatch was due to be on stage with them but her belly button ring went septic." After landing the award for best international female singer, American singer Sheryl Crow joked: "I want to thank the Spice Girls for not being in my category."
Hype abounds in the pop world but this time around it has been justified.
For the Spice Girls headed a bumper year for the industry with album sales topping 200 million for the first time in 1996 and sales heading for a 10 percent rise this year.
George Michael cemented his comeback by landing the award for Best Male singer while Prince, now renamed The Artist, put in a rare stage appearance in Britain to sing "Emancipation."

Pop's generation gap was bridged by Diana Ross who performed her classic "Upside Down" with soul band Jamiroquai. After 30 years in the pop business and sales that have now topped 100 million, the Bee Gees were given a special "outstanding contribution to music" award.

The British-born Australians, once kings of the disco famed for their falsetto voices, gold medallions and flares, then treated the audience to a medley of their greatest hits from "To Love Somebody" to "Staying Alive."
The veteran trio, who are now back in the charts with another hit single and planning a world tour, have as songwriters notched up a total of 20 number one hits in the United States alone.
